drills.name: Stationary Pound Dribble
drills.instructions: Start in an athletic stance, knees bent, feet about shoulder-width. Pound the ball with the right hand for 20 seconds, then the left for 20 seconds — waist height or lower, controlled with the fingertips, eyes up, stay low. Rest, reset, repeat.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low ball-control, weak-hand control, poor stance, or low dribble confidence. Use lower speed and shorter sets if control slips. No speed challenge until the dribble is steady.
drills.statistic: Youth development builds from basic control, stance, and confidence before adding speed or defenders — a player who can't control a stationary dribble isn't ready for full-speed moves.
drills.safety: Keep the player in control. No speed challenge until the dribble is steady.

drills.name: Low Dribble Control
drills.instructions: In a low athletic stance, dribble below knee height with the right hand for 15 seconds, then the left for 15. Back straight, hips low, eyes up. Control first, not speed. Rest, reset, repeat.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for players who dribble too high or lose the ball under pressure. Allow waist-high dribbles first if low is too hard. Keep the stance strong; stop if knees or back hurt.
drills.statistic: Good handlers change dribble height. A low dribble protects the ball and builds hand strength before crossovers or defense.
drills.safety: Keep the stance strong. Stop if knees or back hurt.

drills.name: Stationary Crossover
drills.instructions: In an athletic stance, dribble the ball low across the body to the other hand and back, keeping it in front. Chest up, knees bent, eyes forward. 20 controlled crossovers, rest, repeat.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for the first dribble move. Use slower, wider crossovers first. Stay balanced — no hard side-to-side lunging yet.
drills.statistic: The crossover is a basic move, but beginners learn control before speed. A clean stationary crossover sets up movement drills later.
drills.safety: Stay balanced. No hard side-to-side lunging yet.

drills.name: Stationary Between-the-Legs Setup
drills.instructions: One foot slightly in front. Dribble the ball from the back hand through the legs to the front hand, then reset the feet and repeat. Start slow, keep it low. 10 reps each side, rest, repeat.
drills.coaching_notes: Best once a basic crossover is controlled. Stay with the stationary crossover if control isn't there. Keep the stance comfortable — don't force a wide split.
drills.statistic: Between-the-legs takes coordination between stance, hands, and timing. Slowing it down teaches the pattern without losing balance.
drills.safety: Keep the stance comfortable. Do not force a wide split stance.

drills.name: Right-Hand Walking Dribble
drills.instructions: Start on a line with the ball in the right hand. Walk forward dribbling at the side of the body, eyes up, steps under control. Go 20–30 ft, turn, come back. Rest, repeat.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for players who can dribble still but lose it while walking. Shorten the distance if the ball gets away. Walk first; no speed until control is steady.
drills.statistic: Players must carry the ball up the floor with control before making moves or reading defenders — walking dribbles are the safest first step.
drills.safety: Walk first. Do not add speed until control is steady.

drills.name: Left-Hand Walking Dribble
drills.instructions: Ball in the left hand, walk forward dribbling on the left side, eyes up. If it gets loose, slow down, regain control, keep going. 20–30 ft, rest, repeat.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for weak off-hand dribbling. Use shorter distance or stationary weak-hand dribbles first. Slow is fine — clean control first.
drills.statistic: Players who use one hand are easy to guard. Building the weak hand early adds options and confidence.
drills.safety: Slow is fine. Clean control first.

drills.name: Cone Dribble Walk
drills.instructions: Set 4–5 cones in a line. Dribble slowly around each with control — strong hand first, then weak hand. Keep the dribble low, eyes up when possible, feet under control. Walk back, rest, repeat.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for learning direction change with the ball. Use fewer cones and wider spacing first. Walk speed first; keep spacing wide.
drills.statistic: Cone dribbling gives a simple target and teaches the body to move with the ball before live defense.
drills.safety: Walk speed first. Keep cone spacing wide enough.

drills.name: Triple Threat Hold
drills.instructions: Catch or start with the ball near the chest. Bend the knees, strong base, ball in the shooting pocket / close to the body, eyes forward. Hold 3 seconds, relax, reset. 8–10 reps.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for offensive stance and ball protection. Use no defense first. Knees bent but comfortable; no contact needed.
drills.statistic: Triple threat connects shooting, passing, and driving — a strong stance gives the player more control.
drills.safety: Keep knees bent but comfortable. No contact needed.

drills.name: Front Pivot Drill
drills.instructions: Start in triple threat; pick a pivot foot. Keep it planted and step around with the other foot to face a new direction, then return. 5 front pivots each direction, reset, switch pivot feet.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for footwork and not traveling. Practice without the ball first if footwork is confusing. Move slowly; keep the pivot foot planted.
drills.statistic: Pivoting keeps players under control, protects the ball, and avoids travel calls.
drills.safety: Move slowly first. Keep the pivot foot planted.

drills.name: Reverse Pivot Drill
drills.instructions: Start in triple threat. Step backward and around with the free foot, turning the body away to protect the ball, keeping the pivot foot down. Reset to triple threat. 5 reps each direction, switch feet.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for protecting the ball and avoiding travels. Do the footwork without a ball first. No defender needed at first; slow and controlled.
drills.statistic: Reverse pivots create space and protect the ball — needed before facing real pressure.
drills.safety: No defender needed at first. Keep it slow and controlled.

drills.name: Wall Shooting Form
drills.instructions: Stand a few feet from a wall, pick a small target. Shoot the ball softly toward it, hold the follow-through, catch, repeat. Smooth and straight. 10–15 reps.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for shooting form without a basket. Use a softer ball indoors if needed. Use a safe wall and enough space; don't throw hard.
drills.statistic: Form can be trained without a hoop — wall form shooting builds clean mechanics and a straight release.
drills.safety: Use a safe wall and enough space. Do not throw the ball hard.

drills.name: Layup Footwork Walkthrough
drills.instructions: A few steps from the basket, no dribble. Right-hand layup: step right, then left, jump and reach the right hand to the rim. Left-hand: step left, then right, reach the left hand. Start slow, finish close, get the ball, repeat.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for learning layup steps. Practice without the ball first if timing is hard. Walk first; no contact or speed until steps are clean.
drills.statistic: Layups are a core beginner scoring skill, and bad steps cause misses or travels — footwork comes first.
drills.safety: Walk first. No contact or speed until steps are clean.

drills.name: Bounce Pass to Wall
drills.instructions: Stand 6–10 ft from a wall. Aim for a spot on the floor about two-thirds of the way to the wall so the ball bounces up to the wall and back. Catch, reset, repeat for 15–20 reps.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for bounce-pass control. Move closer and slow the pass if it's short, hard, or off-angle. Use clear space; no hard passes near others.
drills.statistic: Bounce passes matter for passing around defenders — beginners learn where the ball should hit and how hard to throw it.
drills.safety: Use clear space. No hard passes near other players.

drills.name: Partner Chest Pass
drills.instructions: Two players 8–12 ft apart. Step toward the partner and throw a chest pass; the partner shows hands, catches with two hands, resets, passes back. Call names, pass to the chest. 20 clean passes.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for team passing. Stand closer if passes are weak. Pass to the chest — do not throw at the face.
drills.statistic: Basketball is a team sport; partner passing teaches timing and communication better than solo work alone.
drills.safety: Pass to the chest. Do not throw at the face.

drills.name: Partner Bounce Pass
drills.instructions: Two players 8–12 ft apart. Step forward and throw a bounce pass so the ball hits the floor and rises to the partner's hands; catch, reset, pass back the same way. 20 clean passes.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for bounce passing with a teammate. Move closer and slow down if needed. Keep passes controlled; watch for loose balls.
drills.statistic: Bounce passes get the ball around defenders — beginners learn the right bounce spot and speed with a real partner.
drills.safety: Keep passes controlled. Watch for loose balls.

drills.name: Defensive Stance Hold
drills.instructions: Feet wider than shoulder-width, knees bent, chest up, hands out. Hold 10–20 seconds — coach checks for being too upright, leaning too far forward, or sitting on the heels. Rest, reset, repeat.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for basic defense. Shorten the hold if legs tire. No long holds if knees hurt; keep posture strong.
drills.statistic: Defense starts with stance — a player who can't hold a stance can't slide, close out, or guard the ball.
drills.safety: No long holds if knees hurt. Keep posture strong.

drills.name: Defensive Slide Line Drill
drills.instructions: Start in defensive stance on a line. Slide right 3–5 steps, then back left, without crossing the feet — stay low, chest up, push off the outside foot. 3 rounds, rest, repeat.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for lateral defensive movement. Use slower slides or shorter distance first. Keep distance short; stop if knees, ankles, or hips hurt.
drills.statistic: Slides teach balance, lateral control, and staying between the offensive player and the basket.
drills.safety: Keep distance short. Stop if knees, ankles, or hips hurt.

drills.name: Closeout Walkthrough
drills.instructions: Start near the paint; a cone/coach on the wing. Jog toward it, take short choppy steps near the end, raise one or both hands, and stop balanced in a defensive stance. Backpedal/walk back, repeat.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for approaching a shooter under control. Walk the closeout first before jogging. No contact; no jumping into shooters.
drills.statistic: Closeouts are common on defense — beginners learn control first, because a wild closeout gives up easy drives.
drills.safety: No contact. No jumping into shooters.

drills.name: Right-Side Backboard Touch Finish
drills.instructions: Start on the right block. Step toward the basket, look at the top corner of the square, and lay the ball softly off the backboard. Rebound, reset on the same spot, repeat. Make it touch the glass softly — don't throw it hard. 10 makes, rest, repeat.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low finishing touch, poor backboard aim, or low rim confidence. Move closer / lower the hoop if form slips. No jumping into others; keep under the rim clear.
drills.statistic: Beginners need a clear target near the rim. The backboard gives a simple aiming point and builds close-range consistency before speed or defense.
drills.safety: No jumping into other players. Keep the area under the rim clear.

drills.name: Left-Side Backboard Touch Finish
drills.instructions: Start on the left block. Step toward the basket, look at the square, and lay it up softly. Rebound, reset on the left block, go again. Stay calm — touch, not speed. 10 makes, rest, repeat.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for left-side finishing and weak-hand confidence. Let the player use two hands first if one-hand touch isn't ready. Keep reps slow; no contact or speed yet.
drills.statistic: Players who finish on only one side are easier to guard. Left-side finishing builds balance and confidence around the rim.
drills.safety: Keep reps slow. Do not add contact or speed yet.

drills.name: Two-Hand Soft Finish
drills.instructions: Right under the rim, hold the ball in two hands. Bend the knees, jump lightly, and place the ball softly off the glass or into the rim. Land, rebound, reset, repeat — keep the ball high, finish soft. 10 clean makes.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for younger/smaller players still building close-range strength. Lower the hoop or move closer if strength is an issue. Land on balance; no jumping under someone's feet.
drills.statistic: Some beginners need touch and confidence before one-hand finishes. A two-hand finish gives more control on easy close shots.
drills.safety: Land on balance. No jumping under someone else's feet.

drills.name: Outside-Hand Extension Finish
drills.instructions: Close on the right side, step toward the rim and extend the right hand high toward the backboard — the ball comes up high and soft, not from the waist. Rebound, reset, repeat; then the left side with the left hand. 6 makes each side.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for players who bring the ball low or finish too close to the body. Use a two-hand soft finish if strength is low. No defender yet; keep jumps controlled.
drills.statistic: Finishing high gives a better angle and is harder to block — beginners need high-release habits early.
drills.safety: No defender yet. Keep jumps controlled.

drills.name: One-Step Layup Finish
drills.instructions: Very close to the basket. Take one step with the outside foot, jump, and finish softly off the backboard. Rebound, reset, repeat — right side first, then left. Slow and clean.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for players who take too many steps near the rim. Practice the step without the ball first. No speed yet — clean footwork first.
drills.statistic: Beginners often travel near the rim from panic or unclear steps; one-step finishing simplifies the movement.
drills.safety: No speed yet. Clean footwork first.

drills.name: Two-Step Gather Finish
drills.instructions: A few feet out. Take one controlled dribble, gather the ball with two hands, then two steps into the layup, finishing softly off the backboard. Land controlled, rebound, reset. Both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for the gather step before layups. Use no-dribble gather reps first if timing is hard. Keep the speed slow until footwork is clean.
drills.statistic: The gather is where many beginner layups break down — one dribble, gather, two steps, finish gives a clear rhythm.
drills.safety: Keep the speed slow until footwork is clean.

drills.name: No-Dribble Cut Finish
drills.instructions: Start a few steps from the basket. A passer feeds the ball as the player cuts to the rim; catch, take controlled steps, and finish close. Rebound or rotate out. 8 makes each side.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for off-ball finishing. Use a stationary pass first if catching on the move is hard. Use soft passes; no traffic in the lane.
drills.statistic: Not every finish comes from a dribble — beginners learn to catch, gather, and finish from cuts, a common scoring chance.
drills.safety: Use soft passes. No traffic in the lane.

drills.name: Baseline Cut Finish
drills.instructions: Start near the short corner/baseline; a passer on the wing. Cut toward the basket, show hands, catch, and finish close. Rebound, reset. Reps from both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for simple cuts and close finishes. Walk the cut first before adding speed. No crowding under the rim; keep passes controlled.
drills.statistic: Baseline cuts create simple layup chances — beginners learn to move without the ball and finish right after the catch.
drills.safety: No crowding under the rim. Keep passes controlled.

drills.name: Wing Cut Layup Finish
drills.instructions: Start on the wing; passer at the top or opposite wing. Cut hard to the basket, show both hands, catch, and finish off the backboard. Rebound, pass back out, reset. Both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for wing cuts and rhythm finishes. Start with a walk-through cut if timing is poor. One cutter at a time; no crossing paths under the rim.
drills.statistic: Simple cuts teach beginners that scoring isn't only dribbling — catching on the move and finishing builds game-ready habits.
drills.safety: Use one cutter at a time. No crossing paths under the rim.

drills.name: Elbow Catch and Finish
drills.instructions: Start at the elbow; a passer feeds the ball. Catch, square up, take one strong step to the basket, and finish close — stay under control, don't rush. Rebound, reset, repeat from both elbows.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for attacking from the elbow. Start without a pass (stationary ball) if needed. No defender yet; keep the drive short and controlled.
drills.statistic: The elbow is a common scoring spot — catching there and taking one controlled move to the rim teaches simple attacking habits.
drills.safety: No defender yet. Keep the drive short and controlled.

drills.name: Short Corner Finish
drills.instructions: Start in the short corner with the ball. Take one controlled step toward the rim and finish softly off the backboard. Rebound, reset, repeat — both short corners. Soft and balanced.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for close finishes from side angles. Move closer if angle touch is poor. Watch the baseline; don't step out of bounds during the rep.
drills.statistic: Games create different angles around the rim — short corner finishes teach how the backboard changes by position.
drills.safety: Watch the baseline area. Do not step out of bounds during the rep.

drills.name: Overhand High Finish
drills.instructions: Close to the basket, hold the ball high, take one controlled step, and finish with an overhand layup off the backboard — reach up, don't push from the chest. Rebound, reset, repeat both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for players who need a higher release. Move closer if strength is low. No defender yet; focus on control and reach.
drills.statistic: A higher release finishes cleaner near the basket and builds habits for finishing over taller defenders later.
drills.safety: No defender yet. Focus on control and reach.

drills.name: Catch High Finish High
drills.instructions: A passer tosses softly near the rim. Catch high with two hands, keep it above the chest, and finish right away. Rebound or rotate out. Cue: catch high, finish high. 8–10 makes.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for players who bring the ball low after catching. Use a self-toss if no passer. Soft passes; no contact under the rim.
drills.statistic: Young players lose scoring chances by bringing the ball down — keeping it high makes the finish quicker and safer.
drills.safety: Use soft passes. No contact under the rim.

drills.name: Self-Toss Catch and Finish
drills.instructions: Near the basket, toss the ball softly to yourself off the backboard or into the air. Catch with two hands, land balanced, then finish close. Rebound, reset, repeat. Both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for catch-and-finish reps alone. Use smaller tosses if catching is hard. Toss softly; land balanced before finishing.
drills.statistic: Finishing isn't only the shot — the catch and gather matter. Self-toss reps train those parts without a teammate.
drills.safety: Toss softly. Land balanced before finishing.

drills.name: Rebound Putback Finish
drills.instructions: Under the basket, toss the ball softly off the backboard, jump or reach for the rebound, land balanced, and finish right away — keep the ball high after the rebound. Reset, repeat. 8 makes.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for second-chance finishing. Use no jump first for younger players. No crowding under the basket; land under control.
drills.statistic: Many beginner scoring chances come after rebounds — securing the ball and finishing quickly turns them into points.
drills.safety: No crowding under the basket. Land under control.

drills.name: Two-Foot Putback
drills.instructions: Toss the ball off the backboard, catch the rebound with two hands, land on two feet, bend the knees, and go back up strong — don't drift sideways. Reset, repeat. 8 clean makes.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for players who rush putbacks or shoot off balance. Use a low toss and no jump if landing control is poor. Land first, then jump; no contact.
drills.statistic: Two-foot putbacks teach gathering strength before finishing — safer and cleaner for beginners than off-balance second jumps.
drills.safety: Land first, then jump. No contact.

drills.name: Dotted-Line Floater Touch
drills.instructions: Start near the dotted line or a few steps inside the free throw line. Take one controlled dribble, gather the ball with two hands, step into the paint, and shoot a soft floater with one hand — up with touch, not pushed flat at the rim. Rebound, reset at the same spot, repeat. 8 makes, rest, then switch sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low floater touch, poor paint control, weak close-range feel, or low scoring confidence inside the lane. Assign if the player drives into the paint but gets stuck — not close enough for a layup. Move closer if they cannot reach the rim with soft form.
drills.statistic: Youth finishing programs teach floaters because players need a shot between a layup and a jumper. Breakthrough Basketball, Level Up Basketball, and Hooper University all include floater/runner finishes.
drills.safety: No defender yet. Land balanced and do not drift into another player.

drills.name: Two-Foot Floater
drills.instructions: Start at the lane line with the ball. Take one or two slow dribbles into the paint, gather, land on two feet, bend the knees, and shoot a soft floater. Land balanced, rebound, reset. Stop under control before the ball goes up. 6 makes from each lane line.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor gather balance, low floater accuracy, weak paint footwork, or rushed finishing. Assign if the player shoots floaters while falling forward or off balance. Start with no dribble and a stationary two-foot floater.
drills.statistic: A two-foot gather gives young players more control in the paint — a common teaching step before adding speed, defenders, or advanced reads.
drills.safety: No contact. Make sure the player lands with knees bent and feet under control.

drills.name: One-Foot Runner
drills.instructions: Start near the wing or lane line. Take one or two controlled dribbles into the paint. Near the dotted line, jump off one foot and shoot a soft runner with one hand — eyes on the rim, ball up softly, land under control. Rebound, reset, repeat from both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low runner touch, poor one-foot balance, weak paint scoring, or low finishing variety. Assign if the player drives into the lane but always forces a layup through traffic. Use the two-foot floater first if one-foot balance is poor.
drills.statistic: Runners are common paint finishes for smaller players — they score before reaching shot blockers. Teaching it slowly adds a safe finishing option.
drills.safety: Controlled speed only. Stop if landings get sloppy.

drills.name: Stride Stop Finish
drills.instructions: Start a few steps outside the paint with the ball. Take one dribble, gather, step with one foot, then the second foot into a strong base. Once stopped, go up for a short finish. Land balanced, rebound, reset. Reps from both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor gather control, travel risk, low balance, or rushed close finishes. Assign if the player picks up the ball and takes extra steps or cannot slow down before finishing. Walk through the stride stop without shooting first.
drills.statistic: Player-development libraries separate finishing footwork into stride stops, jump stops, pro hops, and step-throughs. A stride stop gives beginners a clean way to gather without losing balance.
drills.safety: Slow footwork first. No defender until the stop is clean.

drills.name: Pro Hop Gather Finish
drills.instructions: Start just outside the lane with the ball. Take one controlled dribble, gather, and do a small pro hop into the paint. Land on two feet, keep the ball tight, and finish close to the basket. Rebound, reset, repeat both sides. Keep the hop small and controlled.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for weak gather strength, poor paint balance, low two-foot control, or travel risk. Assign if the player gets into the paint but loses the ball or cannot gather cleanly. Use stationary two-foot gathers first if the hop causes travel steps.
drills.statistic: A pro hop teaches players to land strong on two feet. Taught slowly first so the player learns legal footwork and balance.
drills.safety: No contact. Keep the hop small. Land soft and balanced.

drills.name: Pump Fake Step-Through Finish
drills.instructions: Start close to the basket with the ball. Show a controlled pump fake without jumping. Keep one foot planted, step through with the other foot, and finish close to the rim. Rebound, reset, repeat. Both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low patience near the rim, poor pivot control, weak finish footwork, or high travel risk. Assign if the player catches near the rim and rushes the shot even when off balance. Practice the pump fake and pivot without shooting first.
drills.statistic: Step-through finishes connect patience, pivoting, and close-range scoring. The player learns not every finish has to be rushed.
drills.safety: No defender at first. Keep the pivot foot down and land balanced.

drills.name: Pump Fake One-Dribble Finish
drills.instructions: Start near the block or short paint area with the ball. Give a small pump fake, keep the ball protected, take one dribble toward the rim, and finish close. No rushing the fake or extra dribbles. Rebound, reset, repeat both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low fake control, weak one-dribble attack, poor close finish, or low paint confidence. Assign if the player catches close to the basket but cannot create a simple scoring angle. Use the no-dribble pump fake step-through first if dribble control is poor.
drills.statistic: A simple pump fake and one dribble can create a better finishing angle — needed before advanced moves or contact finishes.
drills.safety: No contact. Keep the dribble low and controlled.

drills.name: Same-Foot Same-Hand Finish
drills.instructions: Start close to the right side of the rim. Step off the right foot and finish with the right hand. Then work the left side: step off the left foot and finish with the left hand. Start slow — focus on balance, body control, and soft touch. 5 makes each side.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for coordination, finishing rhythm, one-foot balance, and finish variety. Assign if the player has basic layups but struggles when the step pattern changes. Use close standing finishes first if coordination is poor.
drills.statistic: Defenders time normal layups. Same-foot same-hand finishes build coordination and make the player less predictable.
drills.safety: Slow reps first. No defender until the player lands safely.

drills.name: Off-Foot Outside-Hand Finish
drills.instructions: Start near the right side of the basket. Step off the right foot and finish with the left/outside hand based on the side the coach sets. Begin with a slow walk-through so the player understands the step and hand. Rebound, reset, repeat. Both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low finish adaptability, poor coordination, weak body control, or predictable layup timing. Assign if the player can only finish one way and misses whenever the steps are slightly different. Keep the player very close to the rim at first.
drills.statistic: Game finishes are not always textbook layups. Off-foot work teaches the player to adjust while staying under control.
drills.safety: No speed at first. Do not let the player twist the knee or land off balance.

drills.name: Scoop Finish Walkthrough
drills.instructions: Start a few feet from the basket. Take one slow step toward the rim and scoop the ball upward with one hand — rolling softly off the fingers, high enough to reach the rim. Rebound, reset, repeat both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low finger control, weak scoop touch, poor close-range feel, or low finishing creativity. Assign if the player only throws the ball hard at the rim and has no soft finish. Move closer if they cannot control the ball.
drills.statistic: Scoop finishes teach touch and ball control — useful once the player can make basic close shots.
drills.safety: Close range only. No wild underhand throws.

drills.name: Finger Roll Finish
drills.instructions: Start close to the basket. Step toward the rim and let the ball roll softly off the fingertips — smooth, not pushed from the palm. Rebound, reset, repeat both sides. Start close and slow.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor touch, stiff hands, low close finishing feel, or low finger control. Assign if the player throws layups too hard or shoots close shots with stiff hands. Use a two-hand soft finish first if one-hand control is not ready.
drills.statistic: Touch matters around the rim. Finger roll work helps the player feel the ball leave the hand softly instead of forcing the finish.
drills.safety: No speed or contact until touch is clean.

drills.name: Baby Hook Close Finish
drills.instructions: Start a few feet from the basket on the block. Turn the shoulder slightly toward the rim, keep the ball on the outside shoulder, and shoot a soft baby hook with one hand. Finish high and land balanced. Rebound, reset, repeat both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low hook touch, poor close-range variety, weak paint confidence, or low high-release control. Assign if the player catches near the rim but only knows straight layups. Start closer and use a smaller shooting motion.
drills.statistic: Hook finishes are a common close-range tool, especially near the paint. A baby hook teaches high release and touch without contact.
drills.safety: No defender yet. Keep the turn small and controlled.

drills.name: Middle-Lane Jump Hook
drills.instructions: Start in the middle of the paint with the ball. Take one small gather step, jump straight up, and shoot a hook over one shoulder. Land balanced, rebound, repeat. Work both right- and left-hand hooks if ready.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low paint scoring, weak hook touch, poor vertical balance, or low close-range confidence. Assign if the player gets paint touches but cannot finish unless directly facing the rim. Use the baby hook close finish first if they cannot control the hook motion.
drills.statistic: Jump hooks teach players to score from the paint without a running start, building touch and a higher release near the rim.
drills.safety: Jump straight up and land balanced. No contact.

drills.name: Pivot Hook Finish
drills.instructions: Start on the block with the ball. Keep one foot planted, pivot toward the middle, square the shoulder slightly, and shoot a soft hook. Rebound, reset, repeat. Work both blocks and both hands as the player improves.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low pivot control, poor hook touch, weak post footwork, or low paint confidence. Assign if the player pivots well in place but cannot turn that footwork into a shot. Practice the pivot without shooting first.
drills.statistic: Footwork and finishing have to connect. A pivot hook gives beginners a simple paint move different from a layup or drop step.
drills.safety: No defender first. Keep the pivot foot down and land under control.

drills.name: Seal Catch Finish
drills.instructions: Start near the block with both hands showing as a target. A passer gives a soft pass. Catch, keep the body strong, turn slightly toward the rim, and finish close without bringing the ball low. Rebound or rotate out.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor catch strength, low paint confidence, weak close finish, or low ball security. Assign if the player gets the ball near the rim but fumbles, drops it low, or rushes the finish. Use soft stationary passes first.
drills.statistic: Many close shots start with a catch, not a dribble. Young players need to catch strong and finish before defenders recover.
drills.safety: No contact. Keep passes soft and controlled.

drills.name: Duck-In Finish
drills.instructions: Start just outside the paint. On the coach cue, take one quick step into the lane, show both hands, catch the pass, and finish close to the rim. Rebound or rotate out. Reps from both sides of the paint.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low paint movement, weak catch-and-finish, low positioning awareness, or low rim confidence. Assign if the player stands still in the paint or does not know how to get open close to the rim. Walk the duck-in step first before passing.
drills.statistic: Duck-ins teach simple inside positioning — finishing starts before the catch by stepping into the right space.
drills.safety: No contact. One player at a time near the rim.

drills.name: Short Roll Catch Finish
drills.instructions: Start near the elbow or free throw line. Take two steps toward the basket like rolling to the rim. A passer gives the ball. Catch, gather, and finish close to the basket. Reset and repeat both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low short-roll control, poor catch timing, weak finish balance, or low paint awareness. Assign if the player catches while moving and rushes the finish or fumbles. Use slower walk-in catches first.
drills.statistic: Roll catches are common in team offense. Beginners learn the basic movement and finish before advanced pick-and-roll reads.
drills.safety: No screen contact or defender yet. Keep the movement controlled.

drills.name: Trailer Catch Finish
drills.instructions: Start near half court or the top of the key. Jog down the middle lane toward the basket. A passer gives the ball near the free throw line or paint. Catch, take controlled steps, and finish close. Rebound and reset. Keep the first reps slow.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low transition awareness, poor moving catch, weak finish balance, or low rim confidence. Assign if the player runs the floor but does not know how to catch and finish in rhythm. Start closer to the basket if timing is hard.
drills.statistic: Transition scoring is not always a fast-break layup. Trailer finishes teach players to arrive under control and score off a simple pass.
drills.safety: Jog speed first. No defenders or traffic.

drills.name: Pocket Pass Finish
drills.instructions: Start near the lane line. A passer gives a low pocket pass to the hands. Bend the knees, catch low with two hands, gather to the body, and finish close to the rim. Rebound or rotate out. Both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low catch control, weak low-pass handling, poor gather balance, or low paint finishing. Assign if the player fumbles low passes or brings the ball too far from the body. Use chest-level passes first if low catches are too hard.
drills.statistic: Not every pass near the rim is perfect. Players need to catch low passes and still gather into a clean finish.
drills.safety: Soft passes first. No defenders stepping into the lane.

drills.name: Lob Catch Soft Finish
drills.instructions: A passer tosses a soft lob or high pass near the basket. Catch with two hands, land balanced if needed, and finish softly close to the rim — no slapping at the ball or rushing. Reset and repeat.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low hand-eye coordination, weak high catch, poor close touch, or low rim confidence. Assign if the player struggles catching passes above the chest or rushes high catches near the rim. Use lower soft passes first.
drills.statistic: Good finishers need good hands. High-pass catching near the rim builds confidence and teaches the player to finish after the catch.
drills.safety: No jumping into other players. Keep the lob soft and safe.

drills.name: Put Ball on Rim Finish
drills.instructions: Start close to the basket. Step in slowly and place the ball softly on the front or side of the rim so it rolls in — hand relaxed, finish smooth. Rebound, reset, repeat. Both hands if the player can control it.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor rim touch, hard finishes, low hand control, or low close-shot feel. Assign if the player hits the backboard or rim too hard from close range. Move closer and use two hands if needed.
drills.statistic: Finishing is about touch, not just power. This drill forces the player to slow down and feel the ball near the rim.
drills.safety: No jumping into the backboard support or under other players.

drills.name: Soft Toss Off Glass Finish
drills.instructions: A coach or player tosses the ball softly off the backboard. The finisher catches or gathers the ball after it comes off the glass, then finishes close to the rim — land balanced, keep the ball high. Reset after each rep.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low reaction score, weak hands, poor touch, or low second-chance finishing. Assign if the player struggles with loose balls or rebounds near the rim. Use slower tosses if timing is hard.
drills.statistic: Players do not always get perfect catches near the rim. Soft tosses off glass help players react, gather, and finish without making the drill too physical.
drills.safety: One player under the rim at a time. No crashing for rebounds.

drills.name: One-Dribble Paint Stop Finish
drills.instructions: Start just outside the lane with the ball. Take one strong dribble into the paint, gather, stop with balance, and finish close to the rim. Rebound, reset, repeat both sides. Coach watches for a clean gather and no extra steps.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor drive control, weak gather, low paint balance, or travel risk. Assign if the player drives into the paint but cannot stop and finish cleanly. Use no-dribble stop finishes first.
drills.statistic: Many young players get into the paint and lose control. One-dribble stop finishes teach them to slow down, gather, and score with balance.
drills.safety: No defender. Slow speed first.

drills.name: Step-Around Finish
drills.instructions: Start close to the basket with the ball. Step slightly around the imaginary defender space, keep the ball protected, and finish softly — small, controlled step. Rebound, reset, repeat both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor angle control, low body control, weak ball protection, or limited finishing variety. Assign if the player runs straight into traffic or does not know how to adjust near the rim. Use a floor spot or coach cue for where to step.
drills.statistic: Players do not always need a big move near the rim. A small step-around can create a better angle while keeping the finish simple.
drills.safety: No contact. Keep the step small and balanced.

drills.name: Slow Spin Finish Walkthrough
drills.instructions: Start a few feet from the basket with the ball. Take one slow dribble, plant the foot, turn the body in a controlled spin, gather the ball, and finish close to the basket. Rebound, reset, repeat both sides. The spin should be slow enough to stay balanced.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low body control, poor finishing footwork, weak balance, or low finish variety. Assign if the player has basic finishes down and needs a new controlled move near the rim. Practice the spin without the ball first.
drills.statistic: A spin finish can help players change direction near the rim, but beginners learn it slowly first. Controlled footwork matters more than speed.
drills.safety: No defender. No fast spins until the player can land safely.

drills.name: Backdoor Cut Finish
drills.instructions: Start on the wing; a passer stands near the top of the key. Take one or two steps away from the basket like you are coming to the ball, then quickly cut behind the imaginary defender toward the rim. Show both hands, catch the pass, gather under control, and finish close. Rebound, pass back out, reset. Reps from both wings.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low off-ball movement, weak cutting timing, poor catch control, or low rim confidence. Assign if the player stands still on offense or only tries to score by dribbling. Walk the cut first if timing is hard.
drills.statistic: Beginner players often chase the ball instead of moving into open space. Backdoor cuts teach simple off-ball scoring — timing, spacing, and finishing without over-dribbling.
drills.safety: One cutter at a time. No contact and no crowded lane.

drills.name: Give-and-Go Finish
drills.instructions: Start on the wing with the ball. Pass to a coach or teammate at the top of the key, then cut hard toward the rim. The passer gives the ball back. Catch, gather, and finish close to the basket. Rebound and rotate. Reps from both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low passing movement, poor cutting habit, weak catch-and-finish control, or low team-offense awareness. Assign if the player passes and stands still or does not know how to move after giving up the ball. Walk through pass-cut-catch before adding speed.
drills.statistic: The give-and-go is one of the simplest basketball actions. It teaches a beginner that passing can create their own scoring chance if they move right after the pass.
drills.safety: Use soft passes. Keep the lane clear.

drills.name: Curl Cut Finish
drills.instructions: Place a cone or coach at the elbow as a screen marker. Start on the wing or corner. Run toward the marker, curl tightly around it, show hands, catch the pass near the lane, and finish close to the rim. Stay balanced and do not drift too wide. Reset and repeat both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor movement timing, weak curved cuts, low catch balance, or low finishing rhythm. Assign if the player cuts in straight lines only or catches while drifting away from the basket. Walk the curl first if they lose balance.
drills.statistic: A lot of beginner scoring chances come from simple movement, not advanced dribbling. Curl cuts teach players how to turn a cut into a close finish.
drills.safety: No live screen contact. Use a cone or coach marker only.

drills.name: Rip-Through Straight-Line Finish
drills.instructions: Start on the wing in triple threat. Rip the ball from one side of the body to the other, step past the imaginary defender, take one or two controlled dribbles, and finish close to the rim. Keep the ball tight to the body during the rip. Reset and repeat both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low first-move score, weak ball protection, poor straight-line drive, or low attack confidence. Assign if the player catches and freezes or exposes the ball before driving. Practice the rip-through without dribbling first.
drills.statistic: A rip-through is a basic way to protect the ball and start a drive — needed before advanced moves or live one-on-one finishes.
drills.safety: No defender at first. Keep the drive controlled.

drills.name: Jab Step Drive Finish
drills.instructions: Start on the wing with the ball in triple threat. Give one short jab step with the outside foot, bring the foot back under control, then drive straight toward the rim for a close finish. Keep the ball protected, avoid extra steps, and finish balanced. Reps from both wings.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low triple-threat attack, poor jab control, weak first step, or low drive confidence. Assign if the player catches and dribbles right away without using footwork or balance. Do jab-step-only reps before adding the drive.
drills.statistic: A jab step is one of the simplest ways to create a driving lane. Beginners learn to use footwork before relying on speed or difficult dribble moves.
drills.safety: No defender until the footwork is clean. Do not let the player travel.

drills.name: Hesitation Drive Finish
drills.instructions: Start outside the paint with the ball. Take a controlled dribble toward the basket, give a small hesitation by slowing the body and ball for a second, then drive to the rim and finish. Keep the hesitation simple and balanced. Rebound, reset, repeat both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for one-speed driving, low change-of-pace score, poor body control, or low paint confidence. Assign if the player always drives at the same speed and runs into traffic. Walk through the hesitation first without finishing.
drills.statistic: Players who only go one speed are easier to guard. A hesitation finish teaches beginners how to control pace and attack after a simple pause.
drills.safety: Controlled speed only. No hard stop if knees or ankles hurt.

drills.name: Deceleration Finish
drills.instructions: Place a cone a few feet outside the paint. Dribble toward the cone at a controlled jog, slow down before reaching the paint, gather the ball, and finish close to the rim. Coach cues "slow down before you go up." Reset and repeat both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor deceleration, weak balance, low finishing control, or rushed paint decisions. Assign if the player gets to the rim but cannot slow down enough to finish cleanly. Walk the approach first if stopping control is poor.
drills.statistic: Finishing is not just speed. Players need to slow down, gather, and control the body before the shot. Deceleration work reduces wild misses and bad landings.
drills.safety: No max speed. Land balanced and stop if knee or ankle pain appears.

drills.name: Pool Noodle Extension Finish
drills.instructions: A coach stands near the rim holding a pool noodle straight up or slightly to the side as a safe obstacle. Drive slowly toward the basket and finish around the noodle without touching it — keep the ball high, extend the arm, finish softly. Both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low extension score, weak ball protection, low release height, or poor finish angle. Assign if the player brings the ball into the body or shoots directly into pressure. Hold the noodle farther away if the player is nervous.
drills.statistic: A pool noodle gives a safe visual obstacle. It helps beginners learn extension and ball protection before live defenders are added.
drills.safety: No contact with the coach. Noodle only, no hard objects.

drills.name: Pad Brush Balance Finish
drills.instructions: A coach stands near the lane with a soft pad. Drive slowly toward the basket. As you gather, the coach gives a light brush with the pad on the side of the body. Stay balanced and finish close to the rim. Contact stays light and controlled. Both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low balance through contact, weak finish strength, poor body control, or fear of paint contact. Assign if the player loses balance from small bumps or avoids finishing near bodies. Do no-contact reps if the player cannot land safely.
drills.statistic: Players eventually need to finish with some body pressure, but beginners should start with soft, controlled contact. A pad brush gives feedback without a dangerous collision.
drills.safety: Light pad only. No pushing, no hard bumps, no airborne contact.

drills.name: Low Ball Pick-Up Finish
drills.instructions: Place the ball on the floor near the block or lane line. Start a few steps away, move to the ball, bend the knees, pick it up with two hands, gather the body, and finish close to the rim. Do not bend only at the waist. Reset the ball and repeat both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low gather control, poor loose-ball handling, weak balance, or low second-effort finishing. Assign if the player fumbles low balls or cannot turn a loose ball into a clean finish. Start closer to the rim if they need more control.
drills.statistic: Games create messy catches and loose balls. Players need to bend, gather, and finish without panicking — this builds that habit safely.
drills.safety: Bend the knees. No diving on the floor.

drills.name: Dribble Handoff Finish
drills.instructions: A coach or teammate stands near the wing or slot with the ball. Start a few steps away and cut toward the ball. The passer hands the ball off. Take the ball, turn the corner, take one or two controlled dribbles, and finish close to the rim. Reset and repeat both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low handoff timing, poor catch control, weak turn-the-corner footwork, or low drive-finish score. Assign if the player fumbles handoffs or does not know how to attack after receiving the ball. Walk through the handoff before adding a dribble.
drills.statistic: Handoffs are common in youth offense because they combine passing, cutting, and driving. Beginners need to learn the exchange before live defense is added.
drills.safety: No screens or contact. Keep the exchange slow at first.

drills.name: Wide-Lane Transition Finish
drills.instructions: Start near half court on the sideline lane; a passer stands in the middle. Run wide down the court, receive the pass near the wing or lane line, take controlled steps, and finish close to the rim. Keep spacing wide before cutting in to finish. Both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low transition spacing, poor lane running, weak catch-and-finish control, or low fast-break awareness. Assign if the player runs down the middle every time and crowds teammates in transition. Start closer than half court if timing is hard.
drills.statistic: Transition offense works better when players fill lanes. Wide-lane finishing teaches spacing and gives the player a cleaner angle to the rim.
drills.safety: Jog speed first. No traffic under the basket.

drills.name: Corner Backdoor Finish
drills.instructions: Start in the corner; a passer stands on the wing. Take a small step up like you are coming to the ball, then cut behind the imaginary defender toward the rim. The passer leads with a soft pass. Catch and finish close. Reset and do both corners.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low corner awareness, poor backdoor timing, weak catch finish, or low off-ball scoring. Assign if the player stands still in the corner or only waits for jump shots. Walk the cut before passing.
drills.statistic: Corner players need to know how to score without dribbling. A corner backdoor cut teaches spacing, timing, and a direct finish at the rim.
drills.safety: Keep the baseline clear. No contact under the rim.

drills.name: Slot Drive Finish
drills.instructions: Start in the slot with the ball, between the top of the key and the wing. Take one strong first step, dribble straight toward the paint, gather under control, and finish near the rim. Do not drift sideways. Rebound, reset, repeat both slots.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor drive angle, weak first step, low paint control, or low finishing confidence. Assign if the player starts drives from the slot but curves wide or loses the angle to the rim. Start without a dribble and walk the angle first.
drills.statistic: Different floor spots create different driving angles. Slot drive finishing teaches the player to attack a clear line to the rim instead of drifting into bad space.
drills.safety: No defender at first. Control the speed.

drills.name: Cut, Stop, Finish
drills.instructions: Start on the wing. Cut into the paint, catch a pass, stop on balance, then finish close to the rim. Coach cues the player to land strong before going up. Rebound, pass back, reset. Both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor moving balance, weak catch control, rushed finishes, or low body control. Assign if the player catches while moving and throws the ball up before getting balanced. Walk the cut and stop first without shooting.
drills.statistic: Catching on the move is hard for beginners. This drill separates the cut, the stop, and the finish so the player learns control before speed.
drills.safety: No contact. Stop balanced before jumping.

drills.name: Relocation Cut Finish
drills.instructions: Start in the corner. Relocate up toward the wing for a step or two, then cut hard to the basket. A passer hits the player near the rim. Catch, gather, and finish close. Reset and repeat both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low spacing awareness, poor cut timing, weak off-ball scoring, or low catch-finish control. Assign if the player stands in one spot and does not know how to move before cutting. Walk through relocation first if timing is confusing.
drills.statistic: Small off-ball movement can set up a better cut. Relocation cut finishes help beginners connect spacing, timing, and finishing without needing advanced plays.
drills.safety: One cutter at a time. Keep the lane clear.

drills.name: Shot Pocket Hold
drills.reps_target: 10 clean holds before adding a shot
drills.instructions: Stand close to the basket or in open space with the ball. Bring the ball to the shot pocket, shooting hand under or slightly behind the ball, guide hand on the side. Hold for 2 seconds, relax, reset. Do 10 clean holds before adding a shot. Coach checks the ball is not too low, too far outside the body, or sitting in both palms.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor shot setup, low shooting consistency, weak ball placement, or random shooting motion. Assign if the player starts every shot from a different place or brings the ball across the body before shooting. Use no shot first if they cannot find the pocket consistently.
drills.statistic: A consistent shot starts before the ball leaves the hand. Beginners usually miss because the setup changes every rep. The shot pocket gives one repeatable starting point.
drills.safety: No shooting volume needed at first. Hold, reset, and keep the shoulders relaxed.

drills.name: Guide Hand Freeze
drills.instructions: Stand close to the hoop. Get into shooting position, shoot, and freeze both hands after the release. The shooting hand should finish toward the rim; the guide hand stays quiet on the side and does not turn over. Check the hands, rebound, reset, repeat. 8-10 makes from close range.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for guide-hand interference, crooked release, poor shot direction, or low shooting accuracy. Assign if the ball spins sideways, misses left/right often, or the guide hand crosses over after release. Move very close so the player can shoot without forcing power.
drills.statistic: A pushing guide hand can change the direction of the shot. Freezing the hands after release makes the mistake easy to see and correct.
drills.safety: Stay close. Do not move back until the guide hand stays quiet.

drills.name: Follow-Through Hold Makes
drills.instructions: Start close to the basket. Shoot and hold the follow-through until the ball hits rim, backboard, or net — wrist relaxed, fingers toward the rim, body balanced. Only count makes where the follow-through is held. Make 10 clean shots, rest, repeat.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor follow-through, inconsistent release, low touch, or rushed shooting. Assign if the player shoots and immediately pulls the hand down or turns away from the shot. Use very close range if strength is low.
drills.statistic: Holding the follow-through helps the player repeat the same release and gives the coach a simple way to see if the shot was rushed.
drills.safety: Shoot close enough that the player does not throw the ball.

drills.name: Feet Set Before Shot
drills.reps_target: 8 shots with clean feet per spot
drills.instructions: Start at a short shooting spot. Place both feet under the body, bend the knees, check balance, then shoot. Rebound and return to the same spot. Coach cues "feet first, then shot." Make 8 shots with clean feet before changing spots.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor shooting balance, moving feet, low set-shot accuracy, or rushed shot prep. Assign if the player catches and shoots while drifting, stepping, or falling away. Use no jump and very close range first.
drills.statistic: Beginners need balance before range. If the feet are not set, the shot changes every time. This makes foot control the first priority.
drills.safety: No jumping backward or drifting. Keep the shot short.

drills.name: Square-Up to Shoot
drills.instructions: Start slightly turned away from the basket with the ball. Pivot or step into a square position, point the chest and feet toward the rim, then shoot. Rebound, reset at the same angle, repeat. Do both left-turn and right-turn square-ups.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor alignment, low shot direction, weak footwork, or off-balance shooting. Assign if the player shoots with the body turned sideways or shoulders not facing the target. Practice the square-up without shooting first.
drills.statistic: A straight shot starts with the body facing the target. Square-up work teaches the player to organize feet, hips, shoulders, and eyes before the ball goes up.
drills.safety: Move slowly. Keep the pivot foot controlled.

drills.name: Chair Catch Shot Pocket
drills.instructions: Place a chair or cone at a short shooting spot; start behind it. A coach or teammate passes. Step around the chair, catch, bring the ball straight to the shot pocket, pause one second, then shoot. Rebound and reset. Keep the pass soft and the shot close.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor catch prep, slow shot pocket, low hand readiness, or catch-and-shoot struggles. Assign if the player catches the ball low, bobbles the pass, or takes too long to organize the shot. Remove the chair if the movement is too confusing.
drills.statistic: Catch-and-shoot starts with ready hands and a clean shot pocket. This slows the process down so beginners can learn the catch before speed is added.
drills.safety: Use a safe object. Do not let the player trip over the chair or cone.

drills.name: Self-Spin Catch-and-Shoot
drills.instructions: Stand at a short shooting spot and spin the ball out in front with backspin so it bounces back. Step into the catch, set the feet, bring the ball to the shot pocket, and shoot. Rebound, reset, repeat. Start close before moving farther out.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low solo shooting routine, poor catch rhythm, slow feet, or weak shot prep. Assign if the player needs catch-and-shoot reps but does not have a partner. Use a small toss instead of spin if they cannot control the ball.
drills.statistic: Players need a way to practice game-like shooting without always needing a passer. A self-spin creates a moving catch and helps build rhythm.
drills.safety: Make sure the ball does not roll into other players. Stay close and controlled.

drills.name: Partner Pocket Pass Shot
drills.instructions: A passer stands a few feet away. Show target hands near the shot pocket. The passer gives a soft pass right to the pocket. Catch, bend the knees, and shoot — do not drop the ball to the waist first. Rebound, pass back, repeat.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor catch location, slow release, low shot prep, or weak shooting rhythm. Assign if the player catches and dips it too low before every shot. Move closer or use softer passes if catching is hard.
drills.statistic: A good pass helps the shooter; a good catch helps the shot. Pocket passes teach the shooter where the ball should arrive before the shot begins.
drills.safety: Pass to the hands, not the face. Keep the distance short.

drills.name: Corner Set Shot
drills.instructions: Start in the short corner or beginner corner range (not deep three). Set the feet, bend the knees, bring the ball to the shot pocket, and shoot. Rebound and return to the same corner. Make 6, then switch corners.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low corner shooting confidence, poor spot balance, weak set-shot form, or low angle shooting. Assign if the player only practices straight-on shots and struggles from side spots. Move closer inside the corner if they have to throw the ball.
drills.statistic: Different spots change the angle and sight line. Corner set shots teach beginners to keep the same form from a side location.
drills.safety: Do not shoot from three-point range unless form stays clean.

drills.name: Elbow Set Shot
drills.instructions: Start at one elbow with the ball. Set the feet, look at the rim, bend the knees, and shoot with the same motion every time. Rebound and return to the elbow. Make 6, then move to the other elbow.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low elbow shooting, weak midrange confidence, poor shot balance, or inconsistent set-shot form. Assign if the player can make close shots but loses form from a few steps out. Move closer if they cannot shoot without forcing power.
drills.statistic: The elbow is a common shooting spot in youth basketball — far enough to challenge form but close enough for beginners to keep control.
drills.safety: No long range. Make sure the player is not throwing from the shoulder.

drills.name: Short Wing Set Shot
drills.instructions: Start on the wing, a few steps inside the three-point line or wherever the player can shoot with good form. Set the feet, bend the knees, shoot, hold the follow-through, and rebound. Make 6, then switch wings.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low wing shooting, poor spot-shot confidence, inconsistent form, or weak shooting balance. Assign if the player only shoots from straight in front and struggles from wing angles. Move closer if form breaks down.
drills.statistic: Players need to learn the same shot from different spots. Short wing shooting builds comfort without asking for long-range strength.
drills.safety: Stay within the player’s real range. Clean form first.

drills.name: Top-of-Key Short Shot
drills.instructions: Start near the top of the key, closer if needed. Point the feet and shoulders toward the rim, bring the ball to the shot pocket, and shoot. Hold the finish, rebound, repeat. Make 6 before moving.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor straight-on shooting, low shot direction, weak balance, or inconsistent follow-through. Assign if the player misses left and right often from straight-on shots. Move closer if they cannot shoot with natural form.
drills.statistic: Straight-on shots give the player a clear view of the rim and backboard, making it a useful spot for checking alignment and release.
drills.safety: No deep range. Keep the player inside their strength level.

drills.name: Five-Spot Short Shooting
drills.instructions: Pick five beginner-range spots: short corner, wing, top, opposite wing, opposite short corner. Shoot from each until 2 makes, then move to the next. Stay close enough to shoot with good form. The goal is clean makes, not deep range.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low shooting consistency, poor spot confidence, weak shot routine, or limited shooting comfort. Assign if the player only practices from one spot or loses form when changing locations. Use three spots first if five is too much.
drills.statistic: Spot shooting helps players repeat form from different court angles. Keeping the spots short lets beginners build real makes instead of forcing range.
drills.safety: Stay close. Do not turn it into long-range shooting.

drills.name: Make Two Move One
drills.instructions: Start at a short shooting spot. Make 2 shots before moving to the next spot. If you miss, stay there until 2 makes are done. Use 3-5 beginner-range spots. Reset after every shot and keep the same form.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low make consistency, poor focus, low shooting confidence, or rushed reps. Assign if the player shoots randomly without goals or moves spots too quickly. Use make-1-move-1 for younger players.
drills.statistic: Beginner shooters need goals that reward makes and focus. Make-count drills create a simple standard without making the workout too advanced.
drills.safety: Keep the distance short enough for clean form.

drills.name: Swish Only Short Shot
drills.instructions: Start close to the basket. Shoot short shots and only count makes that go cleanly through the net without hitting the rim hard. Focus on soft arc, relaxed wrist, and holding the finish. Make 5 swishes, rest, repeat.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low arc, poor touch, hard misses, or stiff release. Assign if the shot hits the front rim hard or has very little arc. Stand closer if swishes are too hard at first.
drills.statistic: A softer shot with better arc has more room to go in. Swish-only work gives beginners feedback on touch, not just whether the ball happened to drop.
drills.safety: Do not move back until touch is soft from close range.

drills.name: Backspin Check Shot
drills.instructions: Start close to the basket. After each shot, watch the ball in the air for clean backspin. Shoot with a relaxed wrist and fingers through the ball. Only count makes with good rotation. Rebound, reset, repeat.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor ball rotation, stiff wrist, palm push, or inconsistent release. Assign if the ball spins sideways, has no spin, or comes off the hand unevenly. Start very close and reduce power demand.
drills.statistic: Clean backspin usually means the ball is coming off the fingers better. Rotation gives quick feedback on the release.
drills.safety: Close range only. Do not force wrist motion.

drills.name: Bank Shot Angle Series
drills.instructions: Start a few steps from the basket on the right side. Shoot a short bank shot off the backboard. After making a few, move to the left side and do the same. Aim softly and use the correct angle. Make 5 from each side.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor bank-shot touch, low angle shooting, weak short midrange, or low backboard awareness. Assign if the player shoots every short angle shot straight at the rim and misses hard. Move closer if they cannot hit the glass softly.
drills.statistic: Bank shots are useful from short angles. Beginners who learn the glass early have another simple way to score without needing deep range.
drills.safety: No rushing. Keep the shot short and soft.

drills.name: Free Throw Routine Build
drills.instructions: Step to the free throw line or a closer line if needed. Pick a simple routine: breathe, two dribbles, set the feet, look at the rim, shoot, hold the follow-through. Do the same routine every rep. Shoot 10 free throws and track makes.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor free throw routine, low focus, inconsistent shot prep, or low free throw confidence. Assign if the player rushes free throws or changes the routine every shot. Use a closer line if they cannot reach with good form.
drills.statistic: Free throws reward routine and repetition. A consistent routine helps beginners slow down and repeat the same shot under pressure.
drills.safety: Use the right distance for the player’s strength.

drills.name: Short Free Throw Line
drills.reps_target: reps, move line back over time
drills.instructions: Place a tape mark or cone a few feet in front of the free throw line. Use the free throw routine from that shorter spot. Shoot, hold the follow-through, rebound, repeat. Once the player makes shots with clean form, slowly move the line back over time.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low shooting strength, poor free throw form, low confidence, or forced shooting mechanics. Assign if the player throws free throws from the shoulder or chest because the line is too far. Use an even closer mark if form still breaks.
drills.statistic: Players should not have to ruin their mechanics just to reach the rim. A shorter free throw line lets beginners build the same routine with age-appropriate distance.
drills.safety: Do not force full-distance free throws if the player is not strong enough yet.

drills.name: Free Throw Plus Rebound Reset
drills.instructions: Shoot one free throw using your routine. Get the rebound, walk back to the line, reset the feet, take a breath, and shoot again. Do not rush the next shot. Shoot 10 total and record makes.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor reset habits, low free throw focus, inconsistent routine, or emotional response after misses. Assign if the player misses one shot and immediately rushes the next. Use 5-shot sets for younger players.
drills.statistic: Free throw shooting is also a reset skill. Players need to learn that every shot has its own routine, even after a miss.
drills.safety: Walk to the rebound. No diving or rushing under the rim.

drills.name: Catch, Dip, Shoot
drills.instructions: A passer gives the ball to the shooter at a short spot. Catch, dip the ball slightly to the shot pocket, bend the knees, and shoot. The dip should be small and controlled, not all the way to the waist. Rebound, pass back, repeat.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor shooting rhythm, stiff catch, slow shot prep, or low catch-and-shoot accuracy. Assign if the player catches and pauses too long or shoots with no rhythm. Use self-spin catch if no passer is available.
drills.statistic: A small dip can help rhythm if the player controls it. This teaches a clean dip to the shot pocket instead of a big, slow windup.
drills.safety: Keep the shot close. Do not dip so low that form gets slow.

drills.name: Hop Into Set Shot
drills.instructions: Start one small step behind a short shooting spot. Take a small hop into the shot, land on both feet at the same time, bend the knees, and shoot. Keep the hop short and quiet. Rebound, reset, repeat from the same spot.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor foot rhythm, weak shooting base, low catch-and-shoot balance, or inconsistent footwork. Assign if the player catches with feet too narrow, too wide, or pointed away from the rim. Use feet-set-before-shot if hopping causes balance issues.
drills.statistic: Some players shoot better with a small hop into the catch. Beginners need to learn to land balanced before the ball goes up.
drills.safety: Small hop only. Land soft and balanced.

drills.name: One-Two Step Into Shot
drills.instructions: Start one step behind a short shooting spot. Step with the inside foot, then the outside foot, set the base, and shoot. Rebound and reset. Work both sides so the player learns stepping in from different directions.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor shooting footwork, low balance, slow shot prep, or weak catch-and-shoot rhythm. Assign if the player cannot get the feet organized before the shot. Walk through the steps without shooting first.
drills.statistic: A 1-2 step is a common way to enter a shot. It gives the player rhythm and helps the body face the rim before the release.
drills.safety: Slow steps first. No drifting forward.

drills.name: Rebound to Short Shot
drills.instructions: Shoot from a short spot. Get the rebound, dribble or carry the ball back to the same spot, set the feet, and shoot again. Do not throw up quick shots while off balance. Do 10 total shots from one spot, then change spots.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor reset habits, rushed shooting, low shooting discipline, or inconsistent form. Assign if the player rebounds and immediately shoots while leaning or off balance. Use fewer reps for younger players.
drills.statistic: Good practice reps matter more than random volume. Rebound-reset-shoot teaches the player to treat every shot as a real rep.
drills.safety: Do not chase rebounds into other players. Reset before each shot.

drills.name: Beat Your Best Short Shooting
drills.reps_target: 10 shots, then try to beat the score
drills.instructions: Pick one short shooting spot. Shoot 10 shots and record makes. After resting, try to beat that number from the same spot — same form, routine, and distance. Once the player beats the score twice, move to a new beginner-range spot.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low shooting focus, low confidence, poor tracking habits, or inconsistent short shooting. Assign if the player practices without counting makes or does not know if they are improving. Use 5-shot rounds for younger players.
drills.statistic: Tracking makes gives beginners a simple goal. It helps the player see progress and keeps practice focused instead of random.
drills.safety: Keep the spot close enough for clean form. No deep shots for the score.

drills.name: Elbow Under Ball Check
drills.instructions: Stand close to the basket with the ball. Before shooting, pause and check that the shooting elbow is under the ball and pointed toward the rim. Once set, shoot a short shot and hold the finish. Rebound, reset, check the elbow again, repeat. 8 clean makes.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor elbow alignment, low shot direction, inconsistent release, or side-spin misses. Assign if the player misses left and right often or shoots with the elbow pointed away from the rim. Move closer if they cannot keep the elbow under the ball without forcing the shot.
drills.statistic: Youth shooting progressions start with form checks before speed or distance. Elbow alignment is a simple body cue that connects to straighter shots.
drills.safety: Do not force the elbow into pain. Keep the shot close and relaxed.

drills.name: Shooting Line Tape Drill
drills.instructions: Place a strip of tape, court line, or flat marker on the floor pointing toward the rim. Stand with the shooting foot and ball lined up with the line. Shoot a short shot, keeping the ball moving straight along the line. Check whether the body twisted or stayed straight. Rebound, reset, repeat for 10 makes.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for crooked shot path, poor body alignment, side misses, or inconsistent release direction. Assign if the player shoots across the face, twists the shoulders, or misses sideways often. Use an existing court line if tape is not allowed.
drills.statistic: A visual line gives beginners immediate feedback — the shot should travel toward the rim, not across the body.
drills.safety: Use flat tape or a safe floor marker. Do not create a tripping hazard.

drills.name: No-Jump Set Shot
drills.instructions: Start close to the basket with both feet planted. Bend the knees, push through the legs, and shoot without leaving the floor. Stay balanced from start to finish. Rebound, reset, repeat. Make 10 clean shots before moving spots.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor balance, low release control, weak set-shot form, or forced jump shooting. Assign if the player jumps sideways, fades, or loses the shot line during short shots. Use a lower hoop or closer spot if they cannot reach with safe form.
drills.statistic: Beginners do not always need a jump shot right away. A no-jump set shot lets the coach clean up balance and release before adding lift.
drills.safety: Stay close. Do not let the player throw the ball from the chest to reach.

drills.name: Knee Bend Lift Shot
drills.instructions: Start close to the basket. Bend the knees first, then lift the body and ball together into the shot — feel the legs help the ball go up. Land or stand balanced, rebound, repeat. Coach cues "bend, lift, shoot." Do 10 clean makes.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low leg drive, weak shooting range, poor rhythm, or arm-heavy shooting. Assign if the player throws the ball from the arms or cannot get power without losing form. Move closer if they still have to throw the shot.
drills.statistic: Good shooting rhythm connects the legs and upper body. Youth coaches teach power from the floor first so players do not build a two-hand push habit.
drills.safety: Keep the knee bend comfortable. No deep squats or forced jumps.

drills.name: Wrist Snap Close Shot
drills.instructions: Start very close to the basket. Shoot a short shot and focus only on the wrist finishing relaxed toward the rim — hand finishing down, like reaching into the basket. Check the wrist, rebound, repeat. Do 10 makes.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor wrist snap, stiff hand, hard misses, or low shooting touch. Assign if the player pushes the ball with a flat hand or cannot get soft touch near the rim. Use a smaller or lighter ball if they cannot control the wrist.
drills.statistic: A relaxed wrist and finger finish help create softer shots. This isolates the end of the shot without adding distance or speed.
drills.safety: No forced wrist motion. Stop if wrist pain appears.

drills.name: Elbow-to-Eye Lift Shot
drills.instructions: Start close to the basket with the ball in front of the body. Slowly lift the shooting elbow and ball up toward eye level, then finish the shot. The ball should move up cleanly, not around the side of the head. Rebound, reset, repeat. Do 8-10 makes.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor ball path, slow release, low shot consistency, or side-swing mechanics. Assign if the player brings the ball around the hip, across the face, or behind the head before shooting. Do the lift without shooting first.
drills.statistic: A cleaner ball path makes the shot easier to repeat. Beginners need a simple lift pattern before quick releases or movement shots.
drills.safety: Keep the motion smooth. Do not force the shoulder.

drills.name: Seams-to-Rim Shot Prep
drills.instructions: Start close to the basket. Before every shot, quickly turn the ball so the shooting hand feels the seams in a comfortable spot. Set the hand, shoot, hold the finish. Rebound, reset the hand placement, repeat. Do not take too long — the goal is awareness, not a slow routine.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor hand placement, inconsistent grip, low release feel, or weak shooting touch. Assign if the hand is on a different part of the ball every shot or the ball comes off unevenly. Let the player shoot without seam focus if it causes overthinking.
drills.statistic: Players do not need a perfect grip every time, but beginners benefit from learning what a clean hand placement feels like. It helps the ball leave the hand more consistently.
drills.safety: Keep the routine short. Do not make the player freeze before every shot.

drills.name: Catch Ready Hands Shot
drills.reps_target: reps, show hands before each pass
drills.instructions: A passer stands close. Start with hands up and ready before the pass. The passer gives a soft pass. Catch with two hands, bring the ball into shooting motion, and shoot from beginner range. Rebound or pass back, repeat. Show hands before every pass.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low catch readiness, poor hand target, slow shot prep, or low catch-and-shoot control. Assign if the player waits for the ball to arrive before getting hands ready. Use slower passes if catching is hard.
drills.statistic: A shot starts before the catch. Ready hands help the player catch clean and shoot in rhythm instead of fighting the ball.
drills.safety: Pass to the hands, not the face. Keep the pass soft.

drills.name: Pass Back Shot Prep
drills.reps_target: 8 makes per spot, then switch sides
drills.instructions: Start at a short shooting spot with a partner. Pass to the partner, immediately get the feet and hands ready, catch the return pass, and shoot. Rebound or rotate. The key is not to relax after passing. Do 8 makes from one spot, then switch sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low pass-and-ready score, slow catch prep, poor shooting rhythm, or low team-offense awareness. Assign if the player passes and stands flat-footed instead of preparing for the return. Stand closer if the return pass is hard to handle.
drills.statistic: Players often get open shots after moving the ball. Passing and getting ready again teaches a simple team shooting habit.
drills.safety: Use controlled passes. Keep spacing clear.

drills.name: Lift From Corner Shot
drills.instructions: Start in the corner without shooting from deep. Move up a few steps toward the wing, catch a pass or pick up the ball from a coach, set the feet, and shoot from beginner range. Move under control and do not drift sideways on the shot. Reps from both corners.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low relocation shooting, poor foot control, weak catch balance, or low corner-to-wing awareness. Assign if the player stands in the corner and does not know how to move into a shot. Walk the lift first without shooting.
drills.statistic: Relocation shooting helps players learn how to move into open space. Beginners should start with short, controlled lifts before game-speed movement.
